background.definition: The American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology defines early pregnancy loss as a nonviable, intrauterine pregnancy with either an empty gestational sac or a gestational sac containing an embryo or fetus without fetal heart activity within the first 12 6/7 weeks of gestation. Early pregnancy loss is used interchangeably with miscarriage and spontaneous abortion.

list.listitem: Spontaneous miscarriage occurs in 12% to 20% of clinically-recognized pregnancies. In a 2021 review, the pooled risk of miscarriage was reported at 15.3% (95% CI 12.5-18.7%) of all recognized pregnancies.
The rate is likely much higher as many pregnancies terminate before they are recognized.
The rate of pregnancy loss after implantation was estimated to be 31% in one landmark trial.
About 80% of miscarriages occur in the first trimester; the frequency of clinically-recognized early pregnancy loss increases with increasing age.
Modern estimates suggest approximately 25% of reproductive-aged women experience a miscarriage during their lifetime.

The 2021 review article referenced above estimated a population prevalence of women who have had one miscarriage of 10.8% (10.3-11.4%), two miscarriages 1.9% (1.8-2.1%), and three or more miscarriages 0.7% (0.5-0.8%).
Miscarriage is the most common complication of human gestation.

A history of miscarriage (OR 1.45, 95% CI 1.2-1.8) or recurrent miscarriage (OR 2, 95% CI 1.1-3.5) is associated with an increased risk of coronary heart disease.Early miscarriage is also associated with type 2 diabetes (HR 1.2, 95% CI 1.1-1.3) and late miscarriage (12-19 weeks) with an increased rate of type 2 diabetes (HR 1.4, 95% CI 1.1-1.6) and hypertension (HR 1.15, 95% CI 1.05-1.25).

Authors of a meta-analysis including 13 cohort studies and 8 case-control studies found an increased risk of non-gestational diabetes (RR 1.2, 95% CI 1.02-1.3) and gestational diabetes (RR 1.6, 95% CI 1.3-2) for patients ever experiencing a miscarriage compared to those never experiencing a miscarriage.

In a planned secondary analysis of a randomized trial of medical management of early pregnancy loss, 24% of the 275 women scored above 20 on the Center for Epidemiological Studies-Depression scale indicating likely major depression 30 days after treatment. The risk for major depression was twice as high for Black compared to non-Black women (adjusted OR 2.48; 95% CI 1.28-4.81).

The risk of completed suicide is higher among women who experienced a prior fetal loss within 1 year. The adjusted OR for women who experienced a miscarriage was 3.8 (95% CI 2.8-5.2) compared to women who had a live birth.
Chromosomal abnormality of the embryo: majority of cases (e.g., nondisjunction, translocations, trisomies incompatible with life/embryonic development).
Coagulation abnormalities (e.g., factor XIII deficiency, factor V Leiden).
Immunologic causes (e.g., antiphospholipid antibody syndrome).
Anatomic causes (e.g., uterine septum). Authors of a meta-analysis of 9 studies found that leiomyoma presence was not associated with increased risk of miscarriage.
Endocrine factors (e.g., luteal phase deficiency causing inadequate endometrial development).

Viral infection may be involved in some cases. Authors of a systematic review identified 184 mothers infected with SARS-CoV-2 and their 190 stillborn or late miscarriage fetuses. Most cases of fetal demise occurred within approximately 6-13 days after diagnosis or onset of symptoms, and most placentas (88%) were positive for SARS-CoV-2 or presented histologic features of placentitis (massive fibrin deposition and chronic intervillositis).
Possibly environmental factors (e.g., heavy metal exposure).

Based on a large-scale genetic association analyses with 69,054 cases, miscarriage is partly driven by genetic variation potentially related to placental biology. These authors found one genome-wide significant association for sporadic miscarriage (rs146350366, OR 1.4) and three genome-wide significant associations for multiple consecutive miscarriage (rs7859844, OR 1.7; rs143445068, OR 3.4; and rs183453668, OR 3.8).

Authors of two different meta-analyses suggested that −634G/C and +936C/T polymorphisms and certain endothelial nitric oxide synthase gene polymorphisms were associated with risk of recurrent miscarriage; other studies have found single nucleotide polymorphism in the phosphodiesterase 8B gene, p53 polymorphism at codon 72, and interleukin-10 rs1800896 carrying increased risk of recurrent miscarriage.
Similarly, authors of a meta-analysis found a 2-fold increase in miscarriage where sperm showed high levels of DNA damage/fragmentation compared to low DNA damage.

Another study found methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase promoter hypermethylation was more frequent in semen samples from couples with recurrent miscarriage than infertile couples without a history of recurrent miscarriage.
Early pregnancy failure can be further defined on the basis of the pathophysiology of fetal demise.
Anembryonic pregnancy: the trophoblast has invaded the decidual lining but the embryonic disc has not developed.
Embryonic demise: the embryonic disc developed with a subsequent loss of viability.

It appears that endometrial receptivity can also be a factor. In one cohort study, women with a history of recurrent miscarriage had significantly higher level of endometrial proinflammatory cytokines and a reduced expression of anti-inflammatory and angiogenic cytokines during the implantation window than fertile women based on endometrial biopsy samples.

Authors of a meta-analysis including 60 articles found significantly increased uterine natural killer cell levels in endometria of patients with recurrent miscarriage or recurrent implantation failure.

In a histopathological study, compared with tissue from elective abortions, diffuse decidual leucocytoclastic necrosis was found more often in chromosomally normal miscarriages and decidual natural killer cell aggregates was found more commonly in chromosomally abnormal miscarriages. These findings suggest that defective placentation and abnormal maternal immune response are associated with miscarriage.
Several thrombophilic gene polymorphisms are associated with recurrent pregnancy loss. Human leukocyte antigen-G and -F are also associated with recurrent miscarriage and implantation failure.

list.listitem: Identification of risk factors with subsequent appropriate interventions may decrease the risk of miscarriage. C

Modifiable risk factors for miscarriage include the use of tobacco, caffeine, cocaine, and alcohol; optimizing diet; occupational exposures and work conditions; coagulopathies; diabetes; and overweight or underweight maternal status. A

Recent evidence suggest oral progestins may not be effective for treatment of threatened miscarriage. B,, Vaginal progestins do not appear to be effective at reducing the rate of pregnancy loss or live birth in patients with a threatened miscarriage.
Screen for risk factors including the use of tobacco, alcohol, or cocaine at the initial prenatal visit.
Obtain history of any previous blood clots or any family history of coagulopathy.
Determine body mass index.
Evaluate for metabolic syndrome or polycystic ovarian syndrome.
Screen for diabetes (gestational or pre-existing).
Limit or eliminate tobacco use, alcohol use and abuse, high caffeine intake (>5 or >7 cups of coffee or the equivalent per day), and cocaine use.

A diet abundant in fruit, vegetables, seafood, dairy, eggs, and grain may be associated with a lower risk of miscarriage. Conversely, a diet rich in processed food was associated with an increased miscarriage risk (OR 1.97, 95% CI 1.4-3.3).

Prepregnancy body mass index outside the range of 18.5 to 24.9 also increases risk and is potentially modifiable. However, pre-pregnancy weight loss while increasing pregnancy rates does not appear to increase live birth rates or reduce miscarriage rates.
Vitamin supplementation in early pregnancy does not prevent miscarriage; however, taking multivitamins plus iron and folic acid was associated with reduced risk for stillbirth.
There is no evidence to support the recommendation of bedrest for women with threatened miscarriage.

Tight blood pressure control (target diastolic blood pressure, 85 mm Hg) was no different than less tight control (target diastolic blood pressure, 100 mm Hg) on risk of pregnancy loss, high-level neonatal care, or overall maternal complications in an open international, multicenter trial involving 987 women with nonproteinuric preexisting or gestational hypertension. Severe hypertension, however, developed in more women in the less-tight-control group (40.6% vs. 27.5%).
Tight blood sugar control with oral hypoglycemics or insulin may decrease the risk of miscarriage in women with diabetes.

Metformin is prescribed by some physicians for women with insulin resistance (e.g., polycystic ovarian syndrome) and it may reduce the risk of miscarriage, but there are insufficient data to prove efficacy.
Evidence supporting human chorionic gonadotropin for prevention of miscarriage is equivocal as only studies of low quality demonstrate benefit.
Levothyroxine given from pre-conception to delivery to euthyroid women with thyroid peroxidase antibodies did not result in a higher rate of live births than placebo in one RCT with 952 women.

Antibiotic treatment of bacterial vaginosis in low-risk pregnant women did not reduce risk of late miscarriage at 16-21 weeks or spontaneous very preterm birth in an RCT of 2869 low-risk pregnancies; this composite primary outcome occurred in 1.2% of women receiving clindamycin and 1.0% of women receiving placebo.
There is no difference in type of instrument used for chorionic villus sampling and subsequent miscarriage.
Although cesarian delivery has been associated with increased risk of miscarriage in a subsequent pregnancy (aOR 1.37, 95% CI 1.2-1.5), most of this risk can be explained by other known risk factors.

For women with dichorionic triamniotic triplets, expectant management is a reasonable choice when the top priority is a liveborn infant, while fetal reduction can reduce the rate of severe preterm delivery.
Treatment of men with varicocele repair may decrease miscarriage rates.
Data on the potential benefit of progesterone for preventing miscarriage among pregnant women with vaginal bleeding are conflicting.

Based on a meta-analysis of 5 small trials with 660 women with threatened miscarriage, the progestin dydrogesterone was more effective than bedrest or placebo in reducing miscarriage (13% for active treatment vs. 24% among control women; OR 0.47; 95% CI 0.31-0.7).

A 2025 Cochrane review included 8 RCTs and found no difference in miscarriage rates with progesterone supplementation (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.76-1.07). This was a change from the 2018 Cochrane review on the same topic that found a small benefit. Authors of a 2021 meta-analysis of 9 RCTs including 4907 patients found progesterone supplementation reduced the rate of miscarriage (RR 0.70, 95% Cl 0.52-0.94).

However, authors of a 2024 meta-analysis of 15 RCTs found conflicting results. For the 3 RCTs reporting on threatened miscarriage in 1973 patients with a prior history of miscarriage, progesterone possibly increased live births (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.97-1.16, absolute increase 4.4%; low certainty evidence). In the four RCTs including 2540 patients with threatened miscarriage and no prior history of miscarriage, there was no apparent benefit (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.96-1.1, absolute increase 1.7%; very low certainty).

A 2019 RCT included 4153 women with a potentially viable fetus who presented with bleeding before 12 completed weeks gestation and found no difference in live births at 34 or more weeks between those randomized to 400 mg vaginal suppositories or identical placebo twice daily from enrollment to 16 completed weeks (75% [1513/2025] vs. 72% [1459/2013], respectively). There was benefit of progesterone among the 285 women with a history of 3 or more miscarriages, with more women in the intervention group having successful outcomes (72% [98/137] vs. 57% [85/148]); this deserves further study.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 10 trials of progestogen vs. placebo given to women with vaginal bleeding before 24 weeks' gestation, found that oral (NNT = 10), but not vaginal, administration was effective for increasing live birth rates and reducing miscarriages. Since the number of trials of oral progestogen was small (n = 4; 520 participants), a larger trial of oral progestogen was suggested.

It is possible that type of progestin – dydrogesterone vs. natural progesterone – as well as route of delivery - oral vs. vaginal - may be responsible for observed differences in benefit. It should be noted that dydrogesterone is not available in the US or UK, but is marketed in many parts of the world.

Use of progesterone therapy compared to placebo/controls in women with recurrent miscarriage may reduce the number of miscarriages (average RR 0.7, 95% CI 0.5 to 1.0, 10 trials, 1684 women, moderate-quality evidence) and may improve live birth rates (RR 1.07, 95% CI 1.0 to 1.1, 6 trials, 1411 women, moderate-quality evidence). However, in an RCT of daily use of intravaginal progesterone vs. placebo during the first trimester by 836 women with a history of unexplained recurrent miscarriage, there was no difference in live birth rate.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 5 small RCTs with 596 women with a history of recurrent miscarriage found supplementation with human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG) significantly reduced miscarriage, but the results were no longer significant when the two studies with weaker methodology were removed.

In one RCT, preconception aspirin given to women who had experienced 1 or 2 pregnancy losses did not prevent subsequent pregnancy loss. The study results are compromised by a mid-course change to expand enrollment; trial participants tended to be white and had higher incomes and more education.

Interestingly, in a RCT of 1228 pregnant women aged 18 to 40 years of age with 1 to 2 prior pregnancy losses, women randomized to low-dose aspirin had a higher proportion of male live birth than women in the control group (RR 1.31; 95% CI 1.07-1.59). This suggested to the authors that aspirin may modulate inflammation that would otherwise reduce the conception or survival of male embryos.

In another RCT of 1228 otherwise healthy women with one to two prior pregnancy losses who were actively attempting to conceive, use of low-dose aspirin increased live birth rates among women with high baseline serum high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (CRP) (59% vs. 44% in control women) but had no effect on women with mid or low-level CRP.
Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 3 RCTs found enoxaparin treatment has no influence on miscarriage or live birth rate.

Use anticoagulation (i.e., aspirin, heparin) for women with known clotting disorders (e.g., antiphospholipid antibody syndrome) and recurrent miscarriage or a history of blood clots; authors of a Cochrane review found that the combination of unfractionated heparin and aspirin reduced pregnancy loss by 54% among women with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, although trial quality was not high. Patients with known clotting disorders should be managed by an obstetrician specializing in high-risk pregnancies (e.g., a maternal-fetal medicine specialist).

Anticoagulants have NOT been found to be effective for women with recurrent miscarriage without antiphospholipid syndrome. In addition, authors of a recent meta-analysis of 8 trials failed to show benefit of low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) vs. no LMWH in women with inherited thrombophilia and prior late (≥10 weeks) or early (<10 weeks) pregnancy loss.

Among patients with idiopathic recurrent miscarriage, oral immunosuppressants (cyclosporine A, prednisone) were shown to reduce miscarriage rate (OR 0.2, 95% CI: 0.08-0.5) and increase live birth rate (OR 3.6, 95% CI: 2.1-6.2) based on a meta-analysis of 5 studies with 554 patients. Authors, however, noted significant study heterogeneity (I2 = 73%) and moderate-to-severe risk of bias.
IV immunoglobulin treatment was not effective in women with recurrent miscarriage.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis including 8 studies with 1042 patients (485 in the groups receiving either cyclosporine or tacrolimus and 557 women in control groups), intervention patients had increased live birth rate (OR 2.5, 95% CI 1.9-3.3), clinical pregnancy rate (OR 2.2; 95% CI 1.5-4.4) and decreases in miscarriage rate (OR 0.5, 95% CI 0.3-0.6) compared to control patients.

Etanercept, a biopharmaceutical that acts as a tumor necrosis factor inhibitor, was effective in preventing miscarriage in an RCT of 188 patients with at least 4 consecutive miscarriages caused by innate immunity disorders; live birth rates were 89% for women in the intervention group vs. 72% in the placebo group (OR 3.3; 95% CI 1.49∼7.32).

Surgery can correct uterine anomalies (e.g., remove uterine septum). However, there have been no RCTs supporting metroplasty for women with a septate uterus over expectant management. A 2024 guideline from the American Society for Reproductive Medicine concluded that in a patient with infertility, prior pregnancy loss, or poor obstetrical outcome it is reasonable to consider septum incision based on limited evidence.

Women with a history of three or more second-trimester pregnancy losses or extreme premature deliveries, in whom no specific cause other than potential cervical insufficiency is identified, should be offered elective cervical cerclage at 12 to 14 weeks gestation. In one RCT, there was no difference in miscarriage rate between use of a monofilament suture and a braided cerclage suture.
Preimplantation genetic diagnosis for recurrent miscarriage is of unproven efficacy for increasing live birth rates.

Delaying pregnancy: Following a miscarriage, short interpregnancy interval was not associated with increased risk of repeat miscarriage in one study of 514 women; in fact, the 124 women with intervals of less than 3 months had the lowest risk of repeat miscarriage (7.3% vs. 22.1%; adjusted hazard ratio 0.33; 95% CI 0.16-0.71).

Data are insufficient to assess the usefulness of combined estrogen and progesterone for preventing miscarriages. In a meta-analysis of 11 RCT or prospective studies, progesterone plus estrogen for luteal phase support was associated with a higher clinical pregnancy rate than progesterone alone in women undergoing IVF, but there was no difference in miscarriage rate or other outcomes.

Among Chinese women undergoing IVF and embryo transfer who had normal thyroid function but tested positive for thyroid autoantibodies, the use of levothyroxine had no influence on rates of miscarriage or live birth rates.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis concluded that aspirin at 100 mg/d improves the clinical pregnancy rate in women undergoing IVF/ICSI (RR 1.16; 95% CI 1.04-1.28) but had no influence on miscarriage rates or live birth rates.
Common presentations include vaginal bleeding, lack of fetal heart tones, and abdominal pain. C
Serial ultrasounds weekly and serum hCG evaluations every 48 hours are used to confirm a suspected diagnosis of early pregnancy loss (miscarriage). A
Ectopic pregnancy must be excluded by evidence of intrauterine pregnancy. C

list.listitem: Bleeding, lack of fetal heart tones, or abdominal pain are common presentations of early pregnancy failure.
Women with vaginal bleeding during pregnancy that is equal to or greater than that of a regular menstrual flow are 2.6 times more likely to miscarry than women with light bleeding.

In one cohort study, women with a clinically-confirmed pregnancy at 6-8 weeks’ gestation and vaginal bleeding without nausea (3.6% of 701 women) had the highest risk of miscarriage (risk difference 56.1%, positive likelihood ratio 11.1 (2.04, 20.1), and negative likelihood ratio 0.86 (0.79, 0.93).

Uterine size on bimanual exam that is inconsistent with estimated gestational age may suggest miscarriage. However, in one RCT of 135 women with first trimester bleeding presenting to the emergency department, vaginal examination did not improve diagnostic accuracy in conjunction with ultrasound and beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (b-hCG).
Fetal heart rate abnormalities increase the risk of miscarriage.

Transvaginal or abdominal ultrasound is obtained to identify intrauterine pregnancy and cardiac activity. Fetal cardiac activity should be present at a gestational age of 35 days from the last menstrual period and/or when the embryonic pole is greater than 5 mm.

Any of the following signify early pregnancy loss:
Absence of cardiac activity on ultrasound in an embryo exceeding 7 mm in crown rump length. Absence of an embryo with a heartbeat 2 weeks or more after a scan showing a gestational sac without a yolk sac or 11 days or more after a scan showing a gestational sac with a yolk sac. Absence of an embryo when the mean sac diameter exceeds 25 mm. Additional criteria suggestive of early pregnancy loss can be found in the ACOG bulletin.
Gestational sac diameter should increase by 0.6 mm per day on serial ultrasound in a normally-developing pregnancy.
A discrepancy in gestational sac and crown-rump length or between menstrual and sonographic age of the pregnancy of greater than 1 week increases the risk of miscarriage.
A gestational sac should be seen on ultrasound when b-hCG is greater than 2000 mIU/mL.
Authors of a meta-analysis of 11 studies found echogenic mass to be the most sensitive and specific predictor of retained products of conception after any pregnancy event.

Serum hCG levels are most useful when prompt ultrasound is not available. When used in the assessment or management in a patient with a threatened miscarriage, they should always be drawn serially. A single hCG level is rarely useful.
Serial hCG levels should increase by 53% to 66% every 48 hours in a normal intrauterine pregnancy.

For women with an increase in serum hCG >63% after 48 hours, a viable intrauterine pregnancy is likely. An ectopic cannot be excluded, and this result should be followed with a transvaginal ultrasound within the next 7-14 days.
For those with a decrease of >50%, inform the woman that the pregnancy is unlikely to continue, provide information about support/counseling services, and ask her to take a pregnancy test in 14 days.
Reevaluate women who do not fall into these two categories within 24 hours.
Tests than can be considered include a single serum progesterone level and pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A).

With respect to the former, authors of a meta-analysis of five studies with 1998 women, using cut-off values from 3.2 to 6.0 ng/mL, found that among women with symptoms and inconclusive ultrasound, the progesterone test predicted a non-viable pregnancy with pooled sensitivity of 75%, specificity of 98.4%, positive likelihood ratio of 45, and negative likelihood ratio of 0.26.
A single midluteal serum progesterone measurement was not predictive of the outcome of a subsequent pregnancy in women with unexplained recurrent miscarriage.

In a small study of 42 women with threatened miscarriage and 40 controls, median PAPP-A level was significantly lower in patients with spontaneous abortion (occurred in 11%). A cutoff of 0.66 MoM (95% CI 0.561-0.773) resulted in the best sensitivity (44%) and specificity (93%).

Among women undergoing in vitro-fertilization/intracytoplasmic sperm injection, those with ongoing pregnancies vs. miscarriages had significantly higher estradiol and progesterone serum levels from the 7th day after embryo transfer (mid-luteal phase).

In a meta-analysis of 15 studies with 1263 women with threatened miscarriage, serum CA 125 had high predictive value in identifying continuing pregnancies, with a positive likelihood ratio of 7.86 (95% CI 4.23-14.60) and negative likelihood ratio of 0.10 (95% CI 0.06-0.20). The most commonly used biomarkers, serum hCG and progesterone, were not useful in predicting outcome of a pregnancy with a viable fetus.
Low levels of serum kisspeptin, a neuropeptide that stimulates the release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, are associated with an increased risk of miscarriage.

In one cohort study, the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio was a prognostic factor of early miscarriage with an area under the curve of 0.792 for distinguishing between the missed and threatened abortion groups; the best cutoff value was 5.72.

For women with threatened miscarriage, an alpha fetoprotein concentration ratio in vaginal blood to maternal serum of >13.4 was 100% specific to confirm pregnancy failure with a sensitivity of 73%. Ratios of <4.3 were reassuring.

A rapid test strip detecting both AFP and IGFBP-1 was shown to identify the presence of embryonic or fetal tissue in vaginal blood. In this study, vaginal blood from 14 of the 16 individuals with active miscarriages was correctly positive for embryonic or fetal tissue while vaginal blood from individuals with ectopic pregnancies, threatened miscarriages, and complete miscarriages was negative for embryonic or fetal tissue. This bedside test could aid in diagnosing miscarriage and ruling out ectopic pregnancy (specificity 97.7%, 95% CI 87.7-99.9%).

Cell-free DNA testing on maternal blood can be considered as a non-invasive approach to detecting aneuploidies in clinical miscarriages. In a study including 1000 consecutive women with pregnancy loss diagnosis, the cell-free DNA-based test had a sensitivity for aneuploidy detection of 85% (95% CI 79-90) and a specificity of 93% (95% CI 88-96) compared with direct sequencing of the pregnancy tissue. In a retrospective study, cell-free DNA analysis correctly identified 74/87 (85.1%) of samples (excluding triploidies) compared to analysis of products of conception.

A prediction model for successful expectant management including incomplete miscarriage at primary scan, vaginal bleeding, and maternal age (younger) gave an area under the ROC curve of 0.796 in the initial model and 0.803 in the validation model.
See for a suggested approach to diagnosis, and for a suggested approach to management.

When a miscarriage is suspected based on symptoms, the initial tools for diagnosis include ultrasound (at presentation and weekly if needed) and quantitative serum hCG (every 48 hours if the diagnosis is not clear after imaging). Serial use of these tools is often required to confirm the diagnosis of miscarriage.

The National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE, 2023) guideline suggests the following: (1) provide support and information to women and (with agreement) their partners about care seeking for worsening or new symptoms, the diagnostic and expected treatment process, recovery and future fertility; (2) be aware of the possibility of pregnancy when women present with symptoms (nonspecific or pregnancy/ectopic related); (3) use transvaginal ultrasound to identify a fetal pole, heart beat and location; (4) use expectant management for the first 7 to 14 days as the first-line management strategy for women with a confirmed diagnosis of miscarriage; (5) explore other management options if a woman is at increased risk of hemorrhage or the effects of hemorrhage (e.g., late first trimester, coagulopathy, unable to have blood transfusion) OR she had a previous adverse or traumatic pregnancy experience (e.g., stillbirth, miscarriage, antepartum hemorrhage) OR there is evidence of infection.

A cost model found that offering women more management options than expectant management or surgical uterine evacuation in an operating room reduced the cost per case from US $1274.58 per case to US $1033.29 per case.

Authors of a systematic review and network meta-analysis found surgical and medical management comparable for women in the first trimester of pregnancy. Overall, surgical approaches have the highest success rate of complete miscarriage (96%), followed by medical management (81%) and expectant management (56%) based on 3 Cochrane reviews of 24 studies including 5577 women.

Patients suffering early pregnancy loss now face barriers to the most effective medication (mifepristone followed by misoprostol) and procedural (uterine aspiration) management options. In a study in New Mexico in 2021, of the 35 (83.3%) hospitals that provided information through key informants or public databases, only two provided comprehensive management, defined as access to mifepristone and misoprostol and uterine aspiration in emergency departments, and 24 (68.6%) provided aspiration somewhere within the hospital for early pregnancy loss.

In another study, institutional abortion restrictions within 149 (of 296) US-based obstetrics and gynecology residency programs were the only significant predictor of rigid reliance on imaging guidelines to differentiate between early pregnancy loss and a potentially viable pregnancy (OR 12.3, 95% CI 3.2-47.9). Further, residency programs in states with hostile legislative policies towards abortion reported being significantly less likely to incorporate other factors with imaging criteria in diagnosing pregnancy loss (33% vs 79%), use of mifepristone (32% vs 75%) or offering office-based suction aspiration (48% vs 68%). Pregnant patients need information about where they can go for help if needed.

No evaluation for recurrent failed early pregnancy is needed until after the third consecutive miscarriage. Once this has occurred, a fertility specialist should be consulted to perform an extensive history and physical exam, as well as obtain appropriate laboratory and imaging studies.

Miscarriage can be managed expectantly (reassurance, serial visits), medically (misoprostol), or surgically (vacuum aspiration or dilation and evacuation [D&E]) based on patient preferences and clinical scenarios. In the first trimester, medical and surgical management produce similar outcomes in indirect comparisons. When expectant and medical management fail to successfully complete a miscarriage, surgical management is the definitive treatment, with an overall success rate of 96%.
The success rates for expectant management vary and have been shown to be up to 80%, but the overall rate is 39% to 56%. A

Medical management using misoprostol has a success rate of 81% to 94% (rates vary depending on the dosing regimen used). A For women with missed miscarriage, pretreatment with 200 mg oral mifepristone as compared with placebo before misoprostol modestly increased the rate of passage of the gestational sac within 7 days (24% vs. 17%, respectively). B

Surgical management of miscarriage is the definitive treatment when other management strategies have failed, or as first-line treatment in certain clinical scenarios. Surgical management with vacuum aspiration (<14 weeks of gestation) or D&E (>14 weeks of gestation) has a greater than 95% success. A
Clinical trials demonstrate the safety and efficacy of misoprostol for active medical management of miscarriage. See and .

In an RCT of 180 women with miscarriage, rates of complete miscarriage were 98.1% for surgical evacuation, 70% for medical evacuation and 79.3% for expectant management. There were differences between groups in psychological well-being, depression scores, anxiety level, or fatigue symptoms at treatment and 4 weeks after treatment.

The American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology recommends misoprostol (800 mcg vaginally), with a repeat dose administered no earlier than 3 hours but within 7 days, if there is no response to the initial dose. They also suggest considering a 200 mg oral dose of mifepristone 24 hours before misoprostol, if the drug is available.The UK guidelines from NICE recommend a mifepristone (200 mg orally once) followed by misoprostol 800 mcg vaginally (or orally if unacceptable) for women with missed or incomplete miscarriage.

Misoprostol is dosed vaginally, buccally or orally from 400 to 800 mcg, in one, divided, or multiple doses and success rates range widely from 68% to 94%. Authors of a Cochrane review found use of misoprostol had comparable success rates with respect to complete miscarriage compared to expectant management, but lower success rates compared to surgical evacuation.
Prescriptions for pain medication and anti-emetics should be offered.
Risks of misoprostol are bleeding, nausea, diarrhea, and possible subsequent need for surgical treatment.

Authors of a Cochrane review found low-quality evidence that medical treatment with vaginal misoprostol hastened miscarriage compared to placebo (5 trials) or expectant management (single trial), but was less effective in accomplishing a complete miscarriage compared to surgical management (6 trials, 943 women, average RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.50). Minor side effects reported were primarily nausea and diarrhea.

Similar results were reported in the recent Cochrane network meta-analysis. These authors concluded that all surgical and medical methods for managing a miscarriage were more effective than expectant management or placebo with surgical methods ranked highest. Expectant management or placebo had the highest chance of serious complications, including the need for unplanned or emergency surgery. A subgroup analysis showed that surgical and medical methods may be more beneficial in patients with missed miscarriage compared to those with incomplete miscarriage.

Authors of a meta-analysis of RCTs comparing misoprostol or medical vacuum aspiration for pregnancies of gestational age up to 6/7 weeks and a diagnosis of incomplete abortion found the rate of complete abortion was higher in the aspiration group (OR 0.2, 95%CI 0.07-0.4). Hemorrhage or heavy bleeding was more common in the misoprostol group (OR 3.0, 95%CI 2-4.6), but pain after treatment was more common in patients treated with aspiration (OR 0.6, 95%CI 0.5-0.8).

In a population-based cohort study including 39,856 women dispensed mifepristone-misoprostol as outpatients compared to 65,176 women undergoing outpatient procedural induced abortion, short-term adverse events were more likely to occur after mifepristone-misoprostol. These included higher rates of both serious adverse events (3.3 vs. 1.8/1000 for procedural management, both at 14 weeks' gestation or earlier; RR 1.9, 95% CI 1.4 to 2.4) and any adverse event (28.9 vs. 12.4/1000; RR 2.3, 95% CI 2.1 to 2.6). Rates of serious adverse events were similar for those receiving care at 9 weeks gestation or earlier (3.4 vs 3.3/1000), although rates of any adverse event were higher for those dispensed medication (31.2 vs. 24.9/1000; RR 1.2, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.5).

In an RCT of medical management of 310 women with missed or incomplete miscarriage before 13 weeks, 400 μg of misoprostol was equivalent to 800 μg for completed miscarriage. Fewer women on the lower dose reported fever/rigors and more women in this group reported their decision to undergo medical management as a good decision. The higher dose was associated with a shortened interval to completion and reduced need for a second dose.

In one RCT of 300 women with early pregnancy loss, pretreatment with 200 mg oral mifepristone before 800 mcg vaginal misoprostol increased the likelihood of successful expulsion of the gestational sac (84% vs. 67%, NNT = 6). In a planned secondary data analysis of this trial, no baseline clinical factors were found that predicted treatment success with combination treatment.

In an RCT of 711 women with missed miscarriage by ultrasound within 14 weeks of pregnancy, pretreatment with 200 mg oral mifepristone as compared with placebo before misoprostol modestly increased the rate of passage of the gestational sac within 7 days (24% vs. 17%, respectively).

A retrospective cohort study (n=˜1000) examined a single-institution's rate of retained products of conception after miscarriage. The original protocol included 800 mcg of vaginal misoprostol with a repeat dose after 7 days if an ultrasound showed retained products. This had a failure rate of approximately 25.1%. When a dose of oral mifepristone 200mg was added to the first dose of vaginal misoprostol the failure rate decreased to 17.8%, NNT=14.

Oral letrozole 10 mg daily for 3 days was similarly efficacious as a single dose of oral mifepristone 200 mg as pre-treatment before vaginal administration of misoprostol 800 mcg for the management of missed miscarriage based on an open-label non-inferiority RCT including 294 patients with missed miscarriage. There were no reported differences in side effects.
There is insufficient evidence to support the use of uterine muscle relaxants or antispasmodics for threatened abortion.
Anti-D immunoglobulin should be considered to prevent alloimmunization.

ACOG recommends consideration of at least 50 mcg of anti-D immunoglobulin to unsensitized Rh-negative women after early pregnancy loss, especially it loss occurred later in the first trimester. Women who undergo surgical management of miscarriage should receive Rh-D immune globulin prophylaxis.

The NICE guideline suggests anti-D rhesus prophylaxis (50 mcg) be offered to all Rh-negative women who have a surgical procedure to manage miscarriage but not to women managed medically or who have a threatened or complete miscarriage.
Miscarriage at up to 14 weeks of gestation can be managed with vacuum aspiration, either with manual (up to 12 weeks of gestation) or electric (up through 14 weeks of gestation) vacuum.
Miscarriage after 14 weeks of gestation can be managed with D&E.

Benefits include convenient timing and high success rates, while risks include infection, perforation, cervical lacerations, and uterine adhesions. Overall rates of infection, however, are low (1%-2%).

In a French RCT including 574 patients with incomplete spontaneous abortion who intended to have a future pregnancy, surgical management by hysteroscopy was not associated with more subsequent births during the 2-year follow up or a better safety profile than vacuum aspiration.

Authors of a cost analysis of surgical vs. medical treatment for early pregnancy loss found an increased cost of $336 (US) for a 13% increased efficacy of surgical management. Of the surgical treatments, manual vacuum aspiration (vs. electric vacuum aspiration) was more cost effective than medical management.

There is no evidence supporting antibiotic prophylaxis after D&C, yet many centers use doxycycline, and ACOG recommends a single 200 mg dose of doxycycline 1 hour before surgical management of early pregnancy loss. There was no benefit of a single dose of 400 mg of oral doxycycline plus 400 mg of oral metronidazole over placebo on rates of subsequent pelvic infection in a recent RCT of 3412 women undergoing surgery to complete a spontaneous abortion in Malawi, Pakistan, Tanzania, and Uganda.

With respect to anesthesia, authors of a Cochrane review of 7 small trials found paracervical block (PCB) was not effective vs. sedation/analgesia or no anesthesia/no analgesia (although PCB with lidocaine is more effective than PCB with saline) and opioids caused more frequent postoperative nausea and vomiting than PCB. In one RCT of 111 women undergoing first trimester uterine aspiration under paracervical block, use of gabapentin 600 mg 1-2 hours preoperatively reduced postoperative pain at 10 and 30 minutes without increasing incidence of nausea or emesis.

Authors of one small RCT with 70 patients found intracervical Laminaria more effective than vaginal misoprostol for cervical dilation when inserted the day prior to suction D&C. Laminaria use, however, was more painful during insertion. Misoprostol was associated with more nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and vaginal bleeding.
ACOG recommends providing anti-D immunoglobulin to unsensitized Rh-negative women immediately after surgical evacuation.

Cochrane authors found insufficient evidence demonstrating that psychological support such as counseling is effective in improving psychological wellbeing in women post-miscarriage.

In an RCT of 280 women post-miscarriage, nurse-provided counseling was not more effective than usual care on measures of general health or depression. The intervention may be of benefit for women with high baseline depression scores or high psychological distress scores.
In a 2021 RCT of 104 women who had experienced a miscarriage, providing supportive care and counseling reduced physical, emotional, behavioral, and cognitive grief symptoms.
Expectant management is an alternative to surgical or medical treatments. See and .
The optimal length of time of expectant management is not clear. US guidelines suggest up to 8 weeks before intervening, except in women with excessive bleeding.

NICE recommends expectant management as first-line treatment for 7-14 days for women with a confirmed miscarriage. Other options than expectant management should be explored for women at increased risk of hemorrhage or risk from hemorrhage, previous adverse experience associated with pregnancy, or evidence of infection.

Success rates vary but can be as high as 76%. This variation is likely related to the criteria for determining success (e.g., the time allowed for completion). In 1 meta-analysis, the overall success rate of expectant management was 39%.

A prediction model for successful expectant management including incomplete miscarriage at primary scan, vaginal bleeding, and maternal age (younger) gave an area under the ROC curve of 0.796 in the initial model and 0.803 in the validation model.

Authors of a 2017 Cochrane review of 24 studies with 5577 women with early miscarriage (<13 weeks) found that expectant management and misoprostol are both acceptable alternatives to routine surgical evacuation given the availability of health service resources to support all three approaches.

In a 2012 Cochrane review of expectant vs. surgical management for early pregnancy failure, expectant management was associated with a higher risk of incomplete miscarriage by two weeks (RR 3.98; 95% CI 2.94-5.38) or six to eight weeks (RR 2.56; 95% CI 1.15-5.69). Expectant management was also associated with a greater need for unplanned (or additional) surgery (28% vs. 4%) and more days of bleeding and need for transfusion (RR 6.45; 95% CI 1.21-34.42). Risk of infection and psychological outcomes were similar but costs were lower for expectant management.

Bed rest is routinely recommended for women with threatened abortion although there is no evidence of benefit. One study showed worse outcomes with bed rest compared with continuation of regular activity.

Doula support during office uterine aspiration for failed or undesired pregnancies did not influence satisfaction, emotional response, sense of empowerment, or perceived ability to cope immediately following or 1 month after the procedure; nearly all women receiving doula support, however, reported that this helped with their experience.

Suspected ectopic pregnancy.
Hemorrhage (if bleeding exceeds more than 2 maxi pads per hour for more than 2 hours then the patient should be evaluated for clinical signs of hypovolemia and you should consider hospitalization).
Unstable vital signs or evidence of infection.
Pain management inadequate as outpatient.
Lack of social support.
Long-distance residence/difficulty accessing medical care.
Transfusion for severe anemia or hypovolemia.
Aspiration of incompletely expelled uterine contents following expectant or medical management.
Re-aspiration of hematometra (abdominal pain with intrauterine material seen on ultrasound).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 4 RCTs with 625 patients found use of hyaluronic acid gel reduced the incidence of postoperative intrauterine adhesions after miscarriage (RR 0.44, 95 % CI 0.29∼0.67) and improved subsequent pregnancy rates (RR 1.94, 95 % CI 1.46∼2.60).

Cabergoline at 1 mg once was effective in preventing breast symptoms at day 4 after second-trimester abortion or pregnancy loss based on an RCT including 73 participants. In this trial, significantly fewer intervention patients compared with those receiving placebo reported any breast symptoms (27.8% vs 97.0%, respectively) and fewer reported significant bother (2.8% vs 33.3%). There were no differences in reported side effect between groups.

Up to 76% of failed early pregnancies will successfully resolve without intervention (expectant management). The remaining will have persistent intrauterine fetal material or hemorrhage requiring intervention. A
There may be an increased risk of preterm birth in a subsequent pregnancy after a second trimester miscarriage. B

Resolution of miscarriage without intervention ranges from 39% to 76% within 6 weeks of diagnosis. The remaining women will have persistent intrauterine fetal material or hemorrhage requiring intervention.

Expectant management success rates (no other intervention needed) range from 39% to 76%. A small RCT from Sri Lanka reported expectant management success rates of 90.1% at 1 week and 94.4% at 2 weeks for incomplete miscarriage among women with amenorrhea of <14 weeks and retained products of conception of <50 mm.
Medical management success is up to 94% based on the regimen used.
Surgical management is greater than 95% successful.

Estimated outcome frequencies based on 12,004 patients with a previous second trimester loss were: live birth 81% (95% CI 64-94), miscarriage 15% (95% CI 4-30), and preterm birth 13% (95% CI 6-23). In the included case-control studies, the pooled OR for preterm birth in subsequent pregnancy was 4.5 (95% CI 3.0-6.7). The supporting evidence was rated as low certainty. Authors of a meta-analysis also found a higher subsequent preterm birth rate among those with a history of recurrent pregnancy loss, with a pooled OR of 1.6 (95% CI 1.4-1.8; 18 observational studies; ; I2 = 85.6%).

For all patients who are managed expectantly or medically: Serial quantitative hCG once weekly until the result approaches the limit of sensitivity of the test to ensure completion and rule out molar pregnancy. Repeat ultrasound weekly if symptoms persist or hCG level is not dropping. Discuss contraception options.

NICE guidelines recommend that women take a urine pregnancy test 3 weeks after medical management of miscarriage unless they experience worsening symptoms and to see their health provider to rule out a molar or ectopic pregnancy if the pregnancy test remains positive.

ACOG notes that confirmation of complete expulsion usually includes ultrasound examination, typically within 7 to 14 days after medical management, although serial serum β-hCG measurements can be used if ultrasonography is unavailable.

For patients who are managed surgically: One follow-up visit at 1 to 2 weeks after the procedure is recommended to assess vital signs, bleeding, and emotional state of the patient and discuss contraception options.

For women with recurrent miscarriage, chromosomal microarray analysis of the products of conception appears to increase detection of chromosomal abnormalities over karyotyping but also increases detection of variants of unknown significance.

Genetic testing of tissues following pregnancy loss appears to be of low clinical utility in identifying couples at risk of a future loss. In a study of 6465 referrals for genetic testing of tissue samples, a genetic cause was identified in 47% of miscarriages before 12 weeks' gestation, 14% at 12-24 weeks, and 6% after 24 weeks but in only 0.4% of cases was a balanced parental rearrangement identified representing risk to a future pregnancy.
Early pregnancy loss is common.
Most early pregnancy losses have no known etiology and could not have been avoided.
No evaluation of etiology is needed until after the third consecutive early pregnancy loss.

There is no medical need to delay attempts at conception following an early pregnancy loss. Abstaining from vaginal intercourse for 1 to 2 weeks after complete passage of pregnancy tissue is generally recommended to reduce the risk of infection, but there are no supporting data.

Special considerations are needed for younger adolescents related to the emotional, legal, and social components of unintended pregnancy and pregnancy loss, including attention to confidentiality laws (laws vary by state).
Evaluation for sexual abuse may be relevant.
